# Tidal Locking and the Shaping of Planetary Climates

Tidal locking—the phenomenon where a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period—profoundly influences planetary climates, particularly on worlds orbiting close to their stars. When a planet becomes tidally locked, one hemisphere experiences perpetual day while the other endures eternal night, creating some of the most extreme climate conditions in the universe.

The most dramatic consequence is the temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in continuous stellar radiation, can reach scorching temperatures, while the nightside plunges to frigid extremes. On airless worlds, this divide is absolute. However, planets with substantial atmospheres can moderate these extremes through atmospheric heat transport. Winds circulate from the hot dayside to the cold nightside, redistributing thermal energy and potentially maintaining habitable temperatures across the entire surface.

This atmospheric circulation creates distinctive climate patterns. On tidally locked planets, air heated on the dayside rises and flows toward the nightside, where it cools and sinks, establishing a persistent circulation pattern.
